Hello there! I am a game designer and programmer with an artistic background in Illustration and shading. My primary focus in games is character, camera, and control.
Lantern of SoulsLearn about my custom camera manager and player controls.Explore GameCupid ShooterLearn about my system for managing couples.Explore GameBonevoyageLearn about my camera and dialogue system.Explore GamePowerPlantLearn about my completely solo project.Explore Game

What is BoneVoyage?#You are a train conductor checking for tickets in a train to the afterlife. If someone doesn’t have their ticket, you can grab them by the neck and throw them off the train! Or you can just do that if you feel like it.
Unfortuneatly, our code got lost, but I will do my best to explain what I did and my thought process.
Dialogue System#Within our dialogue system, I wanted the words to print out like a type writer, and I only had it print 2 sentences at a time to have that satisfying feel that visual novels have.
We had an excel spreadsheet with all of the dialogue for the different characters and situations.
Once the dialogue is grabbed, we enter a while loop, thank is while the length of the dialogue doesn’t equal 0, keep going.
We then grab the first 2 sentences of the dialogue and put it in a seperate text, and then delete it from the original dialogue.
In the seperate text, I do a similar process. While the seperate text is not empty, take a single character and add it to the output. This is what makes the typing effect.
Once that inner while done, we go back to the outer while loop and see if there is more in the original dialogue.
Interaction#For press E to interact, you hover over a skeleton you want to interact with. When the mouse is over the skeleton, they get a white highlight to indicate you are in fact hovering over him. Once you press E, you are lerped into a fixed position where you can either uninteract or strangle them.
The camera had to smoothly interpolate to a fixed position
Upon the camera lerping into a fixed position, the location of the player also had to change to the location of the camera.
However, if the player is lerped to a bad spot, they could easily clip through a bench if we are not careful.
I would consider BoneVoyage a strong predecessor to my camera work in Lantern of Souls.
title: BoneVoyage

content:
The Cupid Shooter Vision#You, cupid, are spawned into a mall, but everyone is in a relationship with the wrong person! You must use your break up gun to break couples up, then use your get together gun to… well… get them together!
In this game jam, I was in charge of making a system that keeps track of the healthy couples and toxic couples in the game.
Initialization#The couple manager is initialized by putting our preassigned couples into a map. It just adds every person and their partner, so everyone will show up once as a key and once as a value. That is why when Num of Toxic Couples is set (for the UI display), it takes the length of the couples array and divides by 2.
Couple Breakup#To get couples together, we must break them up.
We first make sure a person is within a couple in the first place. If they are, we get their partner and assign them to the Ex variable. We then remove both couple instances from the array. Fly away then pushes them apart.
We then see if they were in a healthy relationship or not so we can see if we should subtract from the healthy couples number or toxic couple number. We then set the variables to indicate that they are single now.
Couple Assign#logic for adding couple to arrayBut now we get to DTR. We set the suitor, then we check if they’re suitable to be matched with someone. Then if the suitor is the first person we’re matching together, we assign him to Waiting Pawn. If it’s the second person we shoot, we then add them to the couples array.
We then change the sprites depending on if they’re in a healthy or toxic relationship. Then we update the couple numbers again.
title: Cupid Shooter

content:
What does our camera do?#Jump to Player Blueprints
Lantern of Souls is our current senior capstone, and I was tasked with designing the custom camera manager that fit our needs. Our camera is a dynamic 3rd person camera with our player on the third, and his soul to his side. The camera needed to be able to handle:
Smoothly springarming against walls but not smaller objects switching between our dynamic camera to fixed cameras swtiching to first person within cracks, and allowing the player to look around smoothly switching to cinematics such as dramatic quick time events Design of Springarm#The purpose of our spring arm is to prevent the camera from clipping through walls, pushing the camera closer or towards the center. It currently uses three line traces: one from the player’s head to the camera, one from the camera to straight down, and one from the player to the right vector.
The ray shooting from the head will push the camera to the ray’s collision point, but the ray shooting right from the player will push the camera to the center of the player if it colides.
Code BreakdownThe linetrace collision for the springarm is divided into 3 parts. The first linetrace is to see the location of the wall hit. The trace starts above the players head. this is done by getting the actor location and adding (15, 0, 150) to move it above the players head The trace ends 300 centimeters behind the player by subtracting (300, -90, -35) to the actor location and plugging that into the end.
The outhit location is then used to make a new camera offset. I get the actor location, subtracted that by the outhit location to get the length, I then subtract it by 12,12,12 to make the location land before the wall. (if you get the exact location the camera clips through). I unrotate the vector and that is our new desired camera offset.
The second linetrace shoots down from where the camera normally would be without collision, and that sees if there is a floor. If there isn’t a floor, it spring arms. This method is planned to change in the future when we implement tags.
The third linetrace shoots off to the right to prevent the camera from clipping to the right side of a wall. When the line collides, it brings the camera to the center of the player.
Camera States#My camera switches on an enum between various states such as Looking, Fixed Camera, Peek left, Peek Right, Crack Look, and a death cutscene similar to fixed camera. This system has been easy for my team to follow along and adjust elements if needs be.
LookingNormal Looking is how the looking camera typically works. The desired camera offset changes continuously depending on collisions with walls. If the desired camera offset is different from the actual camera offset, the actual offset will lerp to the desired camera offset.This accounts for changes with wall collisions
Lerp into normal looking is how the looking camera works if we need to interpolate into the looking camera. This happens if we need to transition from another camera mode like Fixed Camera.
FixedThis is a camera that stays in a set position. You can choose to lerp to it or not. Typically used for interactables or cutscenes.
It takes in an arrow within interactables and sets that to the desired camera location and rotation.
Above is a function that my team are able to easily call and plug in an arrow any time they make a new interactable. They are also able to decide if they want to lerp to the camera or cut to the camera.
Peek Left/ Peek RightPeek left and peek right shift the camera to either side and allows the player to look around corners. This adds to the stealth a player can utilize. Q allows the player to peek to the left, and E allows the player to peek to the right. Those inputs are handled in the game controller. Peek left and peek right simply lerp the actual camera offset to a position that is off to the side. It takes the current desired camera location and adds to the Y for peek left and subtracts for peek right. If there is a wall collision that is detected in the Camera orient however, it will interpolate off to the side of the collision location.
Crack LookCrack look started off as a fixed camera that would just switch to peek left and right, which were more fixed cameras. However we wanted the experience in the crack to be more interactive. This is first done by letting the player look around the crack with their mouse.
Then with the quick time event, we wanted something dynamic, which the camera movements had to match. The player is able to look around the corners with the mouse, when the enemy is around the area, and decides to look inside the crack, a quick time event starts.
This is the flow of logic within blueprint update camera. The structure here is similar to the other walking cameras, however instead of camera orient, we have Enter Crack Look, which handles the core logic differently.
Enter Crack look can actually be called within the crack logic. The original rotation is the base rotation for the rest of the logic, and the crack forward vector is plugged into it. We set it to the crack Rotation so that this separate rotation can be plugged into the function in Blueprint update camera.
Normal Crack look around#When the QTE is not active, we have the view where you can look around with your mouse. I grab the crack rotation and use delta rotator to get the difference between the original crack rotation and the control rotation. If the distance is greater than 10, it sets the desired camera offset to face the left, and if its less than -10 it goes to the right. If it’s between those values, it pulls back in the center. The input mouse is there, because if the mouse is fast enough, it won’t pull back to the center.
Afterwards, I set the view max and mins for the pitch and yaw. This locks how far left/right, and up/down you can go with your mouse.
When QTE active#When there’s a QTE, there’s one more boolean for QTE dodging, which happens when the player dodges after successfully doing the QT task. When QTE dodging is active, the QTE direction is chosen by random in the GI_latern, which determines what side of the crack the camera will shift to.
Contributions to the player blueprint#Our player has a soul companion that aids him throughout the level. With that being said, one of the jobs of the soul is to alert the player that a gaurd is near by. When a gaurd is nearby, the soul will hide by the player.
The soul will hide in different sides of the player, specifically on the opposite side of where the gaurd is. The sudden movement of the soul moving alerts the player that something is happening, then the side he’s on helps the player think about their next move.
We were having an issue where the soul would clip into the wall on the right side, so I also made it so where if a linetrace collides on a wall, the soul will move closer to the player.
However, since both of these handles the soul location, I had to incorporate both of them into my logic.
Code BreakdownI first have a custom event that changes the desired soul position, which is used throughout the code.
We then check if the soul is in a cautious state, and if they are not crouching. (crouching has one set location)
If those are true, we then check which side the gaurd is relative to the player(Thiago). The soul has a system that points to the closest gaurd, so we take the rotation of the soul and subtract that from the front vector of the gaurd to see what angle the sould is relative to the player. We then take the z float and see which float range it is within, using the soul placement custom event when one of them is true.
If the soul is in a cautious state, it will then quiver in fear using some sine and cosine waves that I am adding to the desired location. If the soul is not in a cautious state, it will send a linetrace to the right to see if there is a collision. and then lerps next to the player.
title: Lantern of Souls

content:
A fun mini puzzle game with interactables.#This powerplant puzzle game in Unreal is an experience I designed myself from beginning to end. I designed the level, designed the art, and coded the gameplay.
The main thing I want to show for this game is my abilities to create a user experience. Most of the coding handled whether or not players are hitting buttons in the correct order or not, and what objects are in the inventory. (and is a predecessor for code seen in Lantern of Souls)
My idea for this game was to create a point and click experience similar to puzzle games I loved such as Poptropica, while also being satisfying with clicks and clacks on the buttons.
The Center Console#The gameplay is centered on the center console. After each puzzle is solved, another light on the console turns green. The first puzzle you’re most likely to solve is the broken handle. When you are first spawned, you are prompted to add a handle on the floor to your inventory. When you are in front of the console, you drag and drop the handle to the console and PULL THE LEVER.
The second puzzle you might solve is the keypad. When you go to the right of the board, there is a blackboard next to the bookshelf that has a code that Jeffrey decided to write up there. Use that to type in your number and get the next light.
The last puzzle is the soundboard. It is done by going to the casette player and dropping the casette in it. The casette plays an audio that you then try to match on the sound buttons on the console.
Thoughts#Most of the work I have done has been in group projects, but making a game by myself really pushed me to learn more about Unreal, and I was very happy when I pulled it off. I love puzzle games where I can pick up and interact with objects, so this game is very similar to ones I will want to make in the future.
title: The PowerPlant
